passage: At the Christmas prize day, the principal called my name: "Shankar, first in Class 5!" I walked up so proud, holding the shiny book. But back in class, Disha said, "Oh, look, the show-off." Others laughed. At break, someone copied my walk, chin up in the air. I felt my face go hot. I hadn't even been showing off. The next test, I got full marks. When the teacher handed it back, I quickly folded it so nobody could see. When Disha asked my marks, I said, "Okay-okay." I started hiding my good marks every time. I just wanted them to stop. Mummy found a folded paper in my bag and asked why I didn't show her. I didn't know how to explain.

qa.q: What did Shankar get at the Christmas prize day?
qa.a: First in Class 5, with a shiny book.

qa.q: Why did Shankar start folding good test papers?
qa.a: Shankar felt embarrassed and hurt by being called a show-off, and wanted to fit in again by hiding success.

qa.q: How could Mummy help Shankar now that she found the paper?
qa.a: She could ask gently what happened, tell Shankar that doing well is nothing to hide, and maybe talk to the class teacher.

qa.q: How might Disha see Shankar's prize?
qa.a: Disha may have felt envious or left out and used teasing without realising how much it hurt.

grounding: Shows a child mocked as a show-off after winning a prize who starts hiding good marks to fit in.

subtype: Downplaying own success to stay liked [Actor]
passage: Saurabh, okay, you caught me. Yes, I got selected for the national science olympiad. The letter came during Diwali, right when everyone was at our house. Mummy wanted to announce it at dinner and I begged her not to. When my friends asked on the group chat, I wrote, "Lol, fluke, the paper was easy." It wasn't easy. I worked on it for months. But I've seen what happens. When Rohit got into that music school, people started calling him "Mr Big Shot" and stopped inviting him. I don't want that. So I joke about it. But honestly, it feels bad, making my own work sound like nothing. I'm, like, proud and scared at the same time. I, Manoj, am the olympiad guy. And I'm hiding it.

qa.q: When did the olympiad letter arrive?
qa.a: During Diwali, when everyone was at the house.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Manoj describe?
qa.a: Manoj feels proud of the months of work but scared that friends will turn cold and call Manoj arrogant.

qa.q: What could Manoj say to friends that is honest but not boastful?
qa.a: Something like "I worked hard for it and I'm really happy," which owns the success without showing off.

qa.q: How might Saurabh react to hearing the truth?
qa.a: Saurabh might feel pleased to be trusted and glad for Manoj, not seeing it as arrogance at all.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager selected for a national contest downplaying it for fear friends will call them arrogant.

passage: It was the middle of the Buenos Aires winter, and the architecture studio smelled of wet coats. The professor held up Vera's model. "This is the standard for the whole class." Everyone clapped. Mateo clapped too, but something twisted in his chest. They had started the course together. At lunch, when others praised her, Mateo said, "The roof angle's a bit off, though. And she copied the stairs idea from that book." He wasn't sure she had. Later, walking home in the cold, he replayed his words. Why had he said that? He admired the model. He had wanted to ask her how she did the light. Instead he had tried to shrink her. He felt small and a little ashamed.

qa.q: What did the professor call Vera's model?
qa.a: "The standard for the whole class."

qa.q: What was Mateo feeling when he pointed out faults?
qa.a: He felt a sting of envy and fear of being left behind, which turned his admiration into criticism.

qa.q: What could Mateo do instead the next time a peer is praised?
qa.a: He could admit the envy to himself and ask the person how they did it, as he had wanted to ask Vera about the light.

qa.q: How might Vera feel if she heard Mateo's comments?
qa.a: She might feel hurt and confused, since the stairs claim wasn't true and he had clapped for her.

grounding: Shows a young adult who, envious of a praised peer, finds small faults to cut her down.

subtype: Team sniping at the promoted colleague [Observer]
passage: When Sahil was promoted to team lead, Sachin, the department manager, expected some grumbling. He didn't expect the silence. In the team meeting, when Sahil asked for ideas, people shrugged. His messages got one-word replies. At lunch, the old group still ate together, but somehow there was never space for Sahil. Sachin overheard two of them at the tea machine: "Thinks he's our boss now." "He was one of us last week." Nobody was rude. They just quietly stopped helping. Sahil started working through lunch, alone. Sachin realised the team had been comfortable when everyone was equal, and Sahil's rise had upset it. He called the team together that afternoon to talk openly about the change.

qa.q: What did Sachin overhear at the tea machine?
qa.a: "Thinks he's our boss now." "He was one of us last week."

qa.q: What might Sachin be feeling as he watches the team?
qa.a: Sachin seems concerned and uneasy, surprised by the quiet withdrawal rather than open complaints.

qa.q: Why is calling the team together a good step?
qa.a: It brings the unspoken resentment into the open so the team can adjust to the change and support Sahil.

qa.q: What is it like for Sahil after the promotion?
qa.a: Sahil likely feels isolated and confused, working through lunch alone as his old friends withdraw.

grounding: Illustrates a manager noticing a team quietly withdraw support from a newly promoted colleague.

passage: The news reached the kasba by afternoon: Disha had cleared the state government exam. Swati heard it at the bus stand and felt something hot and sour rise in her. They had studied together for two years. Swati had failed by a few marks. For an hour, she sat on the step outside the post office, noticing it. This is envy, she told herself. It's okay to feel it. It's not okay to act on it. She thought of saying, "Well, she had more time," to anyone who'd listen. She didn't. That evening, she walked to Disha's house with a box of pedas. "I'm so proud of you. And a bit jealous, honestly." Disha hugged her. Later Swati asked her, "What did you change in the last months?"

qa.q: What exam did Disha clear?
qa.a: The state government exam.

qa.q: How did Swati handle the feeling that rose in her?
qa.a: Swati recognised it as envy, sat with it for an hour and named it, without letting it turn into criticism of Disha.

qa.q: What did Swati do instead of undermining Disha?
qa.a: She congratulated Disha with pedas, admitted the jealousy honestly, and asked what Disha changed so she could learn for her own goal.

qa.q: How might Disha feel when Swati admits being a bit jealous?
qa.a: Disha might feel touched and trusted, seeing the honesty as a sign of real friendship.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing and naming her envy, then congratulating her friend and asking what the success teaches her.

passage: Before: On Monday, a visiting aunty tried to hold Indu. Indu stiffened and cried, reaching for Amma. During: On Wednesday, Amma sang the same bedtime lullaby, and Indu's eyes grew heavy. Her big cousin Nazia, watching, whispered, "She only sleeps to that song." After: By Saturday, the aunty had visited every day. Indu let her hold her, and even smiled. Nazia laughed. "Now she likes her too."

qa.q: What did Amma sing on Wednesday?
qa.a: The same bedtime lullaby.

qa.q: Why did Indu cry when the visiting aunty tried to hold her on Monday?
qa.a: She felt wary and scared of an unfamiliar face and wanted Amma, who felt safe.

qa.q: What helped Indu accept the aunty?
qa.a: Seeing her every day made the aunty familiar, so she felt safe enough to be held.

qa.q: How does Nazia react to Indu's changes?
qa.a: Nazia notices closely and laughs, amused that Indu now likes the aunty too.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler calmed by a familiar lullaby, wary of a stranger, and warming to her through repeated contact.

passage: It was wedding season in the small town, and at every function the band played the same new film song. The first time Tenzin heard it, at his cousin's mehendi, he wrinkled his nose. "It sounds like a cat." His cousin Bidisha laughed. By the third wedding, he found himself humming it on the way home. By the fifth, he knew all the words. At the last function in February, when the band started it, he jumped up to dance before anyone else. Bidisha raised her eyebrows. "The cat song?" "It's the best song," he said. He wasn't sure when he'd started loving it. He'd just heard it so many times that it felt like his.

qa.q: Where did Tenzin first hear the song?
qa.a: At his cousin's mehendi.

qa.q: How did Tenzin's feelings about the song change?
qa.a: He went from disliking it to loving it, feeling happy and excited enough to dance first.

qa.q: What does this show Tenzin about why he likes some things?
qa.a: That sometimes liking grows from hearing something many times, not only from how good it is.

qa.q: How does Bidisha see Tenzin's change of heart?
qa.a: Bidisha is amused, teasing him about "the cat song" when he jumps up to dance.

grounding: Shows a child who found a tune odd coming to love it after hearing it many times at family functions.

subtype: Warming to a classmate through daily contact [Actor]
passage: When Trisha joined the class in the monsoon term, Kiran didn't like her. She laughed too loudly and always had her hand up. Kiran rolled her eyes at her more than once. But Trisha lived two streets away and took the same bus. Every morning, the bus got stuck in the flooded underpass, and they sat three seats apart, then two, then side by side when the bus got crowded. They didn't talk much at first. Then Trisha offered her umbrella one day. They started talking about a series both watched. By September, Kiran was saving her a seat. She tried to remember why she'd disliked Trisha. She couldn't quite. They had just been around each other every day.

qa.q: Where did the bus get stuck every morning?
qa.a: In the flooded underpass.

qa.q: How did Kiran's feelings toward Trisha change?
qa.a: Kiran went from irritated and dismissive to warm and friendly, saving Trisha a seat by September.

qa.q: What does Kiran's change suggest about first impressions of new classmates?
qa.a: That early dislike can soften with daily contact, so it's worth giving people time.

qa.q: How might Trisha have experienced Kiran's eye-rolling early on?
qa.a: Trisha may have felt unwelcome or unsure, which makes her offering the umbrella quite generous.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who warms to a disliked classmate simply through seeing her daily on the bus and in class.

subtype: Familiar brand mistaken for a better one [Actor]
passage:
Dilnaz: festive sale is on. which earphones r u getting
Urmila: the ones from the cricket ads obviously
Dilnaz: why obviously
Urmila: bcoz they're everywhere. every match, every billboard. they must be good
Dilnaz: have u read any reviews
Urmila: no but i've seen them like a thousand times
Dilnaz: that's not the same as them being good 😅
Urmila: ...ok fair
Dilnaz: my brother has them. he says the mic is terrible
Urmila: hmm
Urmila: why do i trust them so much then
Dilnaz: bcoz ur used to seeing them
Urmila: ok i'll read reviews first. annoying but fair

qa.q: Where has Urmila seen the earphones advertised?
qa.a: In the cricket ads, every match and every billboard.

qa.q: Why does Urmila feel she trusts the earphones?
qa.a: Urmila feels confident about them because they seem familiar from being seen so often, not because of any real evidence.

qa.q: What will Urmila do before buying, and why is it wiser?
qa.a: Read reviews first, because familiarity from ads isn't the same as quality.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see the earphones?
qa.a: Dilnaz is sceptical, pointing out that seeing an advert often isn't proof, and passing on a brother's complaint about the mic.

grounding: Shows a young adult mistaking familiarity from adverts for quality until a friend questions it.

passage: Baljeet, you say you only like Punjabi music and your mother's rajma? Let me tell you what happened to me, when I was a young woman of twenty-four and new in Chennai. I hated the food at first. Everything tasted strange. And the music in the office canteen, I couldn't stand it. Then one day I wondered: do I dislike these things, or are they just unfamiliar? So I made a rule. Three fair tries before deciding. I ate sambar three different days. The second time it was okay. The third, I asked for more. I listened to the canteen songs a whole week. Some I still don't like. But one is still my favourite song today. That's how your Payal Maasi learned to widen her taste.

qa.q: How many tries did Payal give something before deciding?
qa.a: Three fair tries.

qa.q: How did Payal feel about Chennai's food and music at first?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and put off, disliking the unfamiliar tastes and sounds.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Payal widen her taste?
qa.a: Her rule of three fair tries before deciding, which let her tell real dislike from mere unfamiliarity.

qa.q: How might Baljeet respond to Payal's story?
qa.a: Baljeet might feel curious and a little challenged to give new music or food a few fair tries.

grounding: Illustrates an elder recalling how, as a young adult, she gave unfamiliar food and music a few fair tries before deciding.
